text.checkShort: The extra cards are printed and in the loop, and the supermarket has not run empty since.

short.meaning: These loops have fewer cards than the demand over their replenishment lead time needs. When demand runs at its average, the last full container is used before the next one comes back: the line or the pickers wait.
moves: Print the missing cards and put them into the loop with full containers today.
Check the lead time against reality: a milk run that comes every two days instead of daily needs more cards.
Where the cards go missing in the loop, count them at a fixed time each week and replace lost ones at once.
short.question: Which of these loops ran empty in the last month, and how long did the line wait?

excess.meaning: These loops hold more cards than they need: more full containers stand in the supermarket than the demand over the lead time and the safety margin call for. That is money, space and handling tied up, and it hides problems in the loop.
moves: Take the extra cards out one at a time, each when a container comes back, not all at once.
Watch the loop for two weeks after each card taken out: no stock-out, then the next one.
Use the space freed for the parts that need more cards.
excess.question: Why were these cards added: a past stock-out, a longer lead time, or nobody took them out again?

ok.meaning: Every loop has the number of cards its demand, lead time and container quantity call for. Keep it that way: the sizing is only as good as the demand and lead time behind it.
moves: Print the cards and attach one to every full container.
Recalculate every month, or when the demand per day changes by more than about 20%.
Check that every card is in the loop: a lost card is a missing container.
ok.question: Which demand or lead time will change next month, and which loops does it touch?

tips: Use the average demand per working day of the last weeks, in the same days as the lead time. For a part used 2,000 a week on 5 days, D is 400.
L is longer than the transport.

The replenishment lead time runs from the moment a container is emptied to the moment it is back full: the time its card waits to be collected or ordered, plus picking, transport, the supplier or the source process.

Toyota's formula adds a safety factor α to the demand over the lead time. The statistical method sizes the safety stock from the spread of the daily demand (σd) and a service level; a loop without σd falls back to α.
Two containers, each holding at least the demand over the lead time plus the safety stock. When the first is empty, it goes for refill and the second is used.
Enter how many cards each loop has today: the tool shows the cards to add or take out and what it means in stock value.
